newsitem.title: UK: Base metals to see '97 bull market-Credit Lyonnais.
newsitem.headline: Base metals to see '97 bull market-Credit Lyonnais.

text.p: Stronger economic growth next year should stimulate demand for industrial metals and erode stocks, sparking a bull market, broker Credit Lyonnais Rouse said.

"Three combining factors -- rising demand, falling inventories and renewed speculative interest should cause prices to rise ounce again in 1997 as a fundamentally driven bull market takes shape," it said in a research report.
Western economic growth is expected to accelerate next year, with the United States, Germany and Japan forecast to grow by 2.6 percent, 2.3 percent and 3.0 percent respectively, it added.

"Growth in the Asian economies is forecast to stay in the 6.0-9.0-percent range, and with the destocking process of 1996 expected to be reversed in 1997, base metal demand is likely to surprise on the upside," the report said.
"Consequently, given the supply demand dynamics we expect all base metal markets with the exception of copper to move back into deficit in 1997," it said.
But the copper market was currently tight so cash prices should move higher in the short term.

"LME and industry stocks are still only marginally above critical levels (representing just 3.6 weeks of supply), suggesting that prices are currently trading at relatively undervalued levels," the report said.
Cash copper should rise from $2,038 per tonne in the second half of 1996 to $2,250 in the first half of next year, but then start sliding to $2,150 in the second half and $1,900 in 1998.
Aluminium prices should bottom out in the second half of this year before rising to $1,540 in the first half of 1997 and $1,605 in the second half.
Declining prices since the January 1995 high were against a background of fallling consumption and excessive destocking.

"However, the first signs of a sharp rebound in demand are now beginning to emerge and as a result the rising trend in LME inventories should flatten as we move towards the end of the fourth quarter 1996 and into 1997," the repoprt said.

Nickel is seen remaining under pressure in the near term from modestly rising inventories, but even a small turnaround in demand should push the market back into deficit and stocks to critical levels.
Cash prices are seen rallying to $10,000 per tonne in the first half of next year, $14,000 in the second half and $14,500 in 1998.
Total lead inventories should resume their downward trend from early 1997, eroding stock-consumption ratios to 3.7 weeks by the end of 1997 and 3.4 weeks by the end of 1998.

"Cash lead prices should therefore continue to post further gains and could well exceed previous cycle highs of $1,160 and $913 seen in 1978 and 1979 respectively, given that lead inventories are expected to be lower," it said.
Zinc should stay in deficit and stocks should erode by the end of 1997 enough to send prices to $1,200 by the end of that year and $1,500 in 1998.
Tin would have trouble on the upside in the short term from producer selling, but the primary uptrend should continue with prices averaging $6,700 in 1997 and $7,250 in 1998.
